title: {{NAME}} and the Song at the Beginning
moral: The oldest things carry the longest memories, and memory is a kind of magic.

pages.content:
The library's deepest room held a collection nobody was allowed into except the Keeper.

The Keeper was a fairy who had held the position for four hundred years, and she let {{NAME}} in because he was the first researcher in a decade who had asked the right question.

The right question: not what is in there, but what needs to be known from in there.

She took him to the oldest shelf: two items.

A fossilised dinosaur tooth.

A single hair from a unicorn's mane, preserved in amber.

"These are from the same day," she said.

pages.content:
She told him the story.

Four hundred million years ago, give or take, when the last dinosaurs and the first unicorns had existed simultaneously for a brief window, there had been a meeting.

Not an event. A moment: a Triceratops and a unicorn, alone at a water source, recognising each other across an enormous evolutionary distance.

The tooth was from the Triceratops, shed naturally. The unicorn had left a hair in its horn-scratch on a tree.

A fairy had found both and kept them together.

"Why?" asked {{NAME}}.

"Because some moments deserve a witness," she said.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} spent three days studying both objects with the most careful instruments available.

The fairy provided the context he couldn't get from instruments: the quality of the meeting, what the creatures had communicated, the particular quality of that ancient still moment.

He wrote it down in the record book he was given specifically for this purpose.

"You're making it real again," said the fairy.

"It always was real," said {{NAME}}. "I'm making it legible."

pages.content:
On his last day, the fairy said: "There is a living unicorn who carries a memory of that time. Not the memory, but an echo. A resonance."

She took him to the library garden.

The unicorn was old and white and very still. Her horn was silver-grey with age.

When {{NAME}} held up the preserved hair, she went absolutely still for a long moment.

Then her horn pulsed once, warm and ancient.

"She remembers the echo," said the fairy.

{{NAME}} put the hair down gently.

"So do I now," he said.

pages.content:
He walked home in the long autumn evening.

A Triceratops and a unicorn, at a water source, a very long time ago. A fairy noticing and keeping what mattered. A record book now with one more entry.

The world was older than he could feel. The things that had lived in it were more various than he could imagine.

Some of them had met and recognised each other.

He got into bed and looked at the ceiling.

In the dark, he felt it: the very faint resonance of something ancient, still carrying on.
